next_step: Finalize SLO language and reserved GPU sizing; legal to review SLA draft
notes:
Summary:
- Aurora MLworks evaluating Redwood Dedicated for a latency-critical fintech assistant used by traders and ops teams. Primary ask: firm latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) across streaming and non-streaming paths and clear measurement alignment for contractual SLA.

SLO detail discussed (notes from workshop 2026-03-04):
- Target thresholds proposed by Aurora: p50 <= 40ms, p95 <= 120ms, p99 <= 300ms (end-to-end for non-streaming generate calls). Streaming sessions require < 60ms first-byte and steady-state per-chunk <= 30ms for 64-token chunks.
- Important distinction: Aurora wants "client-perceived" timing as the contractual metric. They want the SLA to reflect browser/edge-to-redwood round-trip + server processing + streaming chunk arrival times.
- Redwood position: contractual SLOs are easier to measure server-side (ingress timestamp -> final token send). Proposal: dual reporting — server-side primary metric for SLA credits, client-side sampled synthetic probes for parity and dispute resolution.
- Measurement windows and aggregation: agreed to 5-minute aggregation windows for incident detection, 7-day rolling window for SLO violations, and monthly SLA credit calculation based on calendar-month violation minutes.
- P99 measurement approach: use production-tail sampling (10% of live traffic traced with full timing) plus synthetic probes matching median seq lengths. Avoid relying solely on synthetic tests because batching/kv-cache behavior differs under real traffic.
- Streaming vs non-streaming: define separate SLOs. Non-streaming (single response) and streaming (session/first-byte + steady-state chunk latency). Benchmarks to be expressed both at per-request and per-token levels for long generations.
- Client vs server time: agreed contract language will define primary measurement as server-side ingress->egress with optional client-side probes used for reconciliation; both traces must be stored for at least 90 days (audit requirement).

Throughput & reserved GPU planning:
- Aurora expects peak concurrency of ~1.2k concurrent sessions, average qps 600 with burst to 2k qps during market open. Workload distribution: ~70% short chat (<=128 tokens), 25% retrieval + rerank, 5% long-form summarization (up to 1024 tokens).
- SE recommendation: 8xA10g equivalent nodes with autoscale headroom + 2-node hot-standby pool for safe failover. Suggested reserved commit: 12 GPUs equivalent to match 99th percentile peak throughput with continuous batching disabled for low-latency paths.
- Batching: Aurora requires minimal batching for chat path; Redwood to configure two pools: low-latency pool (no batching, warm KV caches) and high-throughput pool (batching enabled for rerank/embeddings). Routing policy to favor latency pool for pinned routes.

SLA negotiation points to resolve:
- Explicit definition of latency metric (server-ingest vs client-perceived) and which drives credits.
- Treatment of cold starts/warm-up (first 30 minutes after deploy excluded?). Aurora requests shorter exclusion windows for production-critical endpoints.
- How streaming is measured during partial failures or chunk loss.
- Credits formula: Aurora wants linear credits starting at 99.9% monthly SLO; Redwood proposed stepped credits.
